The authors measured coating thermal noise in four different ion-beam sputtered coating samples, including two from Advanced LIGO end test masses and one from an initial LIGO end test mass.
The measured coating thermal noise spectrum did not follow the expected 1/sqrt(f) power-law behavior, but instead had a best-fit slope of around f^-0.45.
At 100 Hz, the coating thermal noise for the Advanced LIGO coatings was (14.0 ± 0.2) x 10^-18 m/sqrt(Hz), slightly higher than the previously reported value.
Extrapolating the measured coating thermal noise to the 6.2 cm beam size on an Advanced LIGO end test mass gives a value of (7.5 ± 0.1) x 10^-21 m/sqrt(Hz) at 100 Hz.
Using the new coating thermal noise measurement, the expected binary neutron star detection range for Advanced LIGO decreases by about 7% from 186 Mpc to 171 Mpc.
The authors estimated the loss angle of the titania-doped tantala coating material used in Advanced LIGO to be (3.6 ± 0.1) x 10^-4, slightly lower than previous reports.
The loss angle of the tantala material in the simpler quarter-wave stack coatings was estimated to be (5.3 ± 0.1) x 10^-4, higher than previously reported values.
The experimental setup used a 3-mirror folded cavity with a near-concentric configuration, producing a waist size of 49 μm and a transverse mode spacing of 133 MHz.
The authors used side-of-fringe locking and active intensity stabilization to mitigate noise sources in the higher-order mode probe beams.
The measured coating thermal noise difference between the two Advanced LIGO coating samples was only 2%, but statistically significant at the 3σ level.
The authors' previous coating thermal noise measurement had a signal-to-noise ratio of only 2 at 40 Hz, while the current experiment had much higher sensitivity.
The new experimental setup allowed the authors to measure coating thermal noise over a much broader frequency range of 30 Hz to 2 kHz.
The authors found that the frequency dependence of the coating thermal noise matched the frequency dependence of the mechanical loss angles reported in previous studies.

The authors note that the new coating thermal noise measurements and their frequency dependence will need to be incorporated into the design and sensitivity projections of future gravitational wave detectors.

The authors attribute the slight difference between their new coating thermal noise measurement and the previous estimate to small systematic effects from the new experimental setup or statistical variations.
